fact: Primary Assessment is the largest current EMT examination domain, accounting for 39–43% of the blueprint.
why: Assessment priorities deserve more study time than isolated trivia.

fact: The current EMT blueprint uses five practice-centered domains: Scene Size-Up and Safety, Primary Assessment, Secondary Assessment, Patient Treatment and Transport, and Operations.
why: The older airway/cardiology/trauma/medical buckets are no longer the EMT exam’s top-level domain structure.

fact: The updated EMR and EMT certification examinations launched April 7, 2025.
why: Study resources written to the older BLS blueprint can now be out of date even when the clinical facts are still useful.

fact: Clinical Judgment is the largest Paramedic examination domain at 34–38%.
why: Paramedic preparation should repeatedly practice recognizing cues, prioritizing problems, choosing actions, and reassessing—not only memorizing facts.

fact: Medical/Obstetrics/Gynecology makes up 24–28% of the current Paramedic examination blueprint.
why: Medical emergencies remain a major content area even with the newer Clinical Judgment domain.

fact: Pediatric patient-care items are integrated throughout the current EMT and Paramedic exam domains instead of existing as one separate pediatric domain.
why: Pediatrics should be practiced across airway, assessment, medical, trauma, treatment, and judgment questions.

fact: Technology Enhanced Items used by the National Registry include build-list, drag-and-drop, and option/check-box formats.
why: Exam preparation should include classifying and ordering information, not only choosing one answer from four options.

fact: The current Paramedic examination is computer adaptive and contains 110–150 questions; 20 are unscored pilot items.
why: You cannot identify the pilot items, so each question should be answered as if it counts.

fact: National Registry says all candidates receive pilot questions; current counts include 10 unscored items for EMT and 20 for Paramedic.
why: Pilot questions help evaluate future items and are mixed into the exam without being identified to the candidate.

fact: National Registry examination content is built from practice analysis and is intended to reflect the tasks, knowledge, skills, and abilities required in current EMS practice.
why: Scenario and priority questions are not a side feature—they are tied to what entry-level clinicians actually do.

fact: For an average adult in cardiac arrest, the 2025 AHA BLS guideline supports a chest-compression rate of 100–120 per minute.
why: Faster is not automatically better; excessive rate can reduce depth and recoil.

fact: For an average adult, AHA recommends compression depth of at least 2 inches (5 cm) while avoiding excessive depth greater than 2.4 inches (6 cm).
why: High-quality CPR is a range of coordinated performance targets, not simply ‘push as hard as possible.’

fact: Before an advanced airway, 30 compressions followed by 2 breaths remains a reasonable adult CPR approach for trained rescuers.
why: Ventilations should be delivered with minimal interruption to compressions.

fact: During an adult cardiac-arrest rhythm check, a healthcare professional should minimize the pulse check to no more than 10 seconds; if a pulse is not definitely felt, compressions should restart.
why: Long pauses reduce chest-compression fraction and interrupt perfusion.

fact: After a shock during adult cardiac arrest, AHA supports immediately resuming chest compressions rather than pausing for a post-shock rhythm check.
why: The goal is to minimize unnecessary interruptions in CPR.

fact: When two or more rescuers are available, switching the chest compressor about every 2 minutes is reasonable.
why: Compression depth commonly deteriorates as a rescuer fatigues.

fact: During adult cardiac arrest, AHA recommends enough tidal volume to produce visible chest rise while avoiding both under- and over-ventilation.
why: More ventilation is not automatically better and can be harmful.

fact: After adult ROSC, once oxygen saturation can be measured reliably, the 2025 AHA guideline considers an SpO₂ target of 90–98% reasonable.
why: Both hypoxemia and unnecessary hyperoxemia should be avoided after resuscitation.
source: American Heart Association — 2025 Post-Cardiac Arrest Care

fact: When a regular narrow-complex tachycardia is causing hemodynamic instability, synchronized cardioversion is a priority treatment in current AHA advanced life support guidance.
why: The key question is whether the tachyarrhythmia is producing the instability—not simply what number is on the monitor.

fact: Sustained polymorphic ventricular tachycardia requires an unsynchronized shock because reliable synchronization to the changing QRS complexes is difficult.
why: This is different from stable or unstable monomorphic rhythms that may allow synchronized cardioversion.

fact: Suspected acute coronary syndrome does not automatically mean routine oxygen when the patient is not hypoxemic.
why: Oxygen should be used for an oxygenation problem rather than as a ritual treatment for every chest-pain patient.

fact: CDC’s current stroke-recognition page uses B.E. F.A.S.T.: Balance, Eyes, Face, Arms, Speech, Time.
why: Posterior-circulation symptoms such as sudden balance or vision changes can be important stroke clues in addition to classic FAST findings.
source: CDC — Signs and Symptoms of Stroke

fact: The time stroke symptoms first appeared—or the last time the patient was known well—is treatment-critical information.
why: Hospital stroke teams use onset/last-known-well time when evaluating eligibility for time-sensitive therapy.
source: CDC — Signs and Symptoms of Stroke

fact: CDC notes that stroke care begins when EMS arrives, and ambulance transport can allow treatment, destination planning, and hospital notification to begin before arrival.
why: A stroke call is not simply transportation; prehospital recognition and communication can shorten delays to definitive care.
source: CDC — Treatment and Intervention for Stroke

fact: A conventional two-wavelength pulse oximeter is not accurate when significant carboxyhemoglobin is present in carbon monoxide poisoning.
why: A normal-looking standard SpO₂ does not rule out carbon monoxide exposure.
source: CDC — Clinical Guidance for Carbon Monoxide Poisoning

fact: In carbon monoxide poisoning, carboxyhemoglobin level does not correlate well with illness severity, outcome, or response to treatment.
why: Exposure history and the patient’s clinical condition still matter even when a COHb number is available.
source: CDC — Clinical Guidance for Carbon Monoxide Poisoning

fact: The National EMS Scope of Practice Model is a national framework; individual states and territories establish the actual legal scope of practice for EMS clinicians.
why: A national study resource should never imply that one medication or procedure is automatically authorized in every EMS system.
source: EMS.gov — National EMS Scope of Practice Model

fact: National Registry explicitly says it does not recommend a particular commercial exam-preparation resource.
why: Use practice questions to identify gaps, then return to your education materials, current national guidance, and local protocols for authoritative learning.

fact: The National Registry EMT exam is computer adaptive: question difficulty changes as the examination estimates whether the candidate meets the passing standard.
why: A hard question during the exam is not evidence that you are failing; focus on the patient problem in front of you.

fact: National Registry sample and real exams can use multiple-response and technology-enhanced formats in addition to traditional single-answer questions.
why: Practicing classification, ordering, and scenario progression can better prepare you for current testing than multiple-choice alone.

fact: The current full American Heart Association CPR and ECC guideline set was published in 2025 and supersedes prior full-guideline recommendations unless a topic was specifically carried forward.
why: Old ‘2020-only’ study sheets should be checked against the current guideline set before being treated as authoritative.
source: American Heart Association — 2025 CPR & ECC Guidelines

fact: Routine mechanical CPR is not recommended for all adults in cardiac arrest in the 2025 AHA BLS guideline.
why: Mechanical devices can have a role in selected situations, but high-quality manual CPR remains the standard default.
